input:
This passage explains the pump affinity laws, a set of relationships describing how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied. The affinity laws relate the performance of a centrifugal pump at one speed to its performance at another speed, for the same pump and the same liquid, and they consist of three proportionalities. Firstly, flow varies in direct proportion to speed, so that at twice the speed the pump delivers twice the flow. Secondly, head varies with the square of speed, meaning that at twice the speed the head rises by a factor of 4. Thirdly, power varies with the cube of speed, so that at twice the speed the power rises by a factor of 8. A helpful worked check is provided by the power law: a speed ratio of 2, when cubed, gives the power ratio of 8, while the head factor of 4 is simply the same ratio squared. In other words, doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies its power draw by 8.

It is important to understand the conditions under which these proportionalities are valid. They describe the pump at corresponding points of its characteristic, where the flow pattern through the impeller is geometrically similar. They are statements about the pump rather than about the system it is connected to, since the duty point the pump actually reaches is determined by the intersection of the pump characteristic with the system resistance, and that intersection does not in general move in proportion to speed. A speed change also leaves efficiency approximately unchanged only near the corresponding point; at speeds far removed from the point at which the laws are anchored, the efficiency shifts and the proportionalities gradually lose accuracy. The laws are applied to the same impeller diameter throughout, as a change of diameter follows different relations, and a change of liquid density leaves flow and head unchanged while scaling power in direct proportion to density.

Used within those limits, the laws allow one measured characteristic to be converted into the characteristic at any other speed, and the cube law is the term that dominates the arithmetic: modest speed reductions deliver disproportionately large power savings, while modest speed increases are paid for at exactly the same rate in reverse.
